authorities.authority: 247 CMR 9.01(2) (Board of Registration in Pharmacy, General Practice Standards), read verbatim in the current official mass.gov publication (running revision date 12/6/24): "A licensee may not process a prescription; dispense a drug, device, or other substance; or administer a controlled substance or vaccine in a manner which is intended, either directly or indirectly, to circumvent any law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy." This is the operative prohibition for the keyed answer. It attaches to the manner in which an arrangement is put together, it expressly reaches indirect circumvention, and it binds "a licensee" rather than only the author of a protocol.

247 CMR 9.01(1) and 9.01(4). Paragraph (1): "A licensee shall conduct professional activities in conformity with M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 24 through 42D, M.G.L. c. 94C, and 247 CMR 2.00: Definitions." Paragraph (4): "A pharmacist shall practice pharmacy within the scope of his or her education, training, and experience and within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice." Paragraph (4) supplies an independent, intent-free basis for the same conclusion, so the keyed answer does not stand or fall on proof of circumvention intent alone. Paragraph (9) ("A licensee may not engage in any fraudulent or deceptive act") was also read and is a distinct standard, correctly kept separate by the dependency rule record.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1. "Administer" is defined as the direct application of a controlled substance, whether by injection, inhalation, ingestion or any other means, to the body of a patient or research subject by a closed list: (a) a practitioner; (b) a nurse at the direction of a practitioner; (c) a registered pharmacist acting in accordance with (i) department regulations, promulgated in consultation with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Department of Mental Health, governing pharmacist administration of medications for treatment of mental health and substance use disorder and at the direction of a prescribing practitioner, (ii) a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care, or (iii) a prescription for the treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted infections, including those defined in regulation by the department pursuant to M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B, or for the prevention of HIV; or (d) an ultimate user or research subject at the direction of a practitioner. The same section defines "Dispense" as delivery to an ultimate user by or pursuant to the order of a practitioner, "including the prescribing and administering of a controlled substance and the packaging, labeling, or compounding necessary for such delivery." The operative act is application to the body, which defeats choice B on the stem's own facts, and administering is a component of dispensing rather than an alternative to it, which defeats choice A's formalism and choice D's conflation of dispensing authority with administration authority.
authorities.exact_section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1, definitions of "Administer" (clause (c)) and "Dispense"

authorities.authority: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 3(6). Schedule VI comprises substances that are prescription drugs and that have not been included in Schedules I through V. An ordinary prescription injectable is therefore a controlled substance in Massachusetts, which is what brings the fact pattern inside the words "administer a controlled substance" in 247 CMR 9.01(2) and inside the s. 1 "Administer" definition. Without this step the keyed reasoning would have a gap, because the stem names no medication and does not say the product is scheduled.

247 CMR 10.03(1) (Grounds for Discipline): "The Board may impose disciplinary action against an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board" on the grounds in M.G.L. c. 112, s. 61 or on enumerated grounds including (b) violating M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 24 through 42A or any provision of state or federal statutes or rules or regulations promulgated thereunder related to the practice of the profession; (e) engaging in misconduct in the practice of the profession; (f) "Engaging in conduct beyond the authorized scope of a pharmacist, pharmacy intern or pharmacy technician"; (l) engaging in conduct that has the capacity or potential to deceive or defraud; and (m) knowingly permitting, aiding or abetting an unlicensed person to perform activities requiring a license. 247 CMR 10.01 confirms the Board may act against a registered pharmacist individually. This defeats choice E: liability under the standard is personal to the licensee who performs the act, and exposure of the protocol's author is additional rather than substitutional.

105 CMR 700.001 and 700.003(6) (Department of Public Health, Implementation of M.G.L. c. 94C). 700.001 defines "Administer" by a list that permits a registered pharmacist or pharmacy intern to administer only "medications for treatment of mental health or substance use disorders and at the direction of a prescribing practitioner," and separately admits "(5) Persons authorized by the Department to administer controlled substances pursuant to 105 CMR 700.003." 105 CMR 700.003(6) provides that "[a] registered pharmacist, pharmacy intern, and pharmacy technician may dispense by administration influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine, and other immunizations designated by the Department to persons five years of age or older," subject to conditions. Read against M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1, this confirms that Massachusetts pharmacist administration authority is enumerated and bounded rather than general, and it identifies a pathway that sits outside s. 1(c) - relevant to the completeness observation recorded in Problem, not to the correctness of the key.
authorities.exact_section: 105 CMR 700.001 (definition of "Administer", clauses (3) and (5)) and 105 CMR 700.003(6)

authorities.authority: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5). In a retail drug business setting, a collaborating pharmacist practising under a collaborative practice agreement is limited to specified activities including "administration of vaccines or the modification of dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician" for the listed conditions. Checked because it is a further Massachusetts pathway by which a pharmacist may lawfully administer outside M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1(c). It does not disturb the key, because the stem stipulates that Massachusetts does not authorize a pharmacist to administer this medication, and because the arrangement described involves no collaborative practice agreement.

247 CMR 2.00 (Definitions). Recorded as a negative finding: the Board's definitional chapter contains no definition of "Administer" and no definition of "Licensee." The controlling definition of the act of administration, and of who may perform it, is therefore the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 / 105 CMR 700.001 definition rather than a separate Board definition, and the reach of the word "licensee" in 247 CMR 9.01(2) is fixed by 247 CMR 10.01 and 10.03(1), which expressly reach an individual registered pharmacist.

results.Problem: No legal error found. The keyed answer C is correct and uniquely correct, and each distractor is defeated by identifiable authority rather than merely being the weaker of two tenable readings. Verification path, performed independently from current official sources on 2026-09-04 and not from the repository's rule summaries: (1) an ordinary prescription injectable is a Massachusetts controlled substance by operation of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 3(6), so both the s. 1 "Administer" definition and the words "administer a controlled substance" in 247 CMR 9.01(2) reach these facts; (2) the operative act under s. 1 is direct application to the body of the patient, and the stem says the pharmacist gives the injection, so the pharmacist is the administering party throughout and choice B fails on the stem's own facts without recourse to any law; (3) s. 1 defines "Dispense" to include "the prescribing and administering of a controlled substance," so administration is a component of the dispensing chain rather than an alternative to it, and labelling the register handover a completed dispensing does not detach the injection from the rules on who may administer - choice A fails, and choice D fails on the same footing because a valid prescription satisfies only routes (ii) and (iii) of s. 1(c) and confers no general administration authority; (4) 247 CMR 9.01(2) is the affirmative prohibition and is written for exactly this manner of arrangement, reaching indirect circumvention and attaching to how the steps are put together rather than to their labels; (5) 247 CMR 10.01 and 10.03(1), which reach "an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board" and list conduct beyond the authorized pharmacist scope as ground (f), defeat choice E. Answer uniqueness is therefore sound, and my independent Phase-1 blind solve, recorded before any canonical content was unsealed, selected C at 0.95 confidence with no second defensible answer set. DEPENDENCY INTEGRITY: verified and intact. The question record hashes to 0f1f0db5e1cb32ee009bcf6959af54d9d4009215a71a82f7afd82be443227ef2, matching the freeze manifest; MA-CONDUCT-ANTI-CIRCUMVENTION recomputes to c0d54e9b61e75f209c5f79644f706b6c43d4c41efd73b46a072424483cd9760b at content_version 1 and MA-ADMINISTER-STATUTORY-ROUTES to 432dee19e2a3691d69193f07a84c78ae54dbe441e610d981699b04bb2f6d2f04 at content_version 1, both matching; the blueprint and style profile likewise match. Both rule records state the law I verified: the anti-circumvention summary is a faithful rendering of 247 CMR 9.01(2), its cross-reference to the separate 247 CMR 9.01(9) fraudulent-or-deceptive-act standard is accurate, and the administration-routes summary accurately reproduces the three clause (c) routes and their differing gates (regulations plus practitioner direction for the mental health and substance use disorder route; a prescription for the testosterone and sexually transmitted infection routes). ACCURACY AND COMPLETENESS OBSERVATIONS, none of which changes the verdict or the key: (a) the explanation's sentence "M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 authorizes pharmacist administration only through the three routes in clause (c)" is accurate as scoped to s. 1, but it is not a complete statement of Massachusetts pharmacist administration authority - 105 CMR 700.001(5) admits "[p]ersons authorized by the Department to administer controlled substances pursuant to 105 CMR 700.003," 105 CMR 700.003(6) authorizes pharmacists, interns and technicians to dispense by administration influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine and other Department-designated immunizations, and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5) permits administration of vaccines under a retail collaborative practice agreement; a reader who took the sentence as an exhaustive map would be misled, and the same gap exists in the MA-ADMINISTER-STATUTORY-ROUTES rule record, which is accurate about the statute it cites but records no pointer to the Department-designated immunization pathway; nothing turns on this here because the stem stipulates the medication is one Massachusetts does not authorize a pharmacist to administer; (b) core_reasoning states that "[p]urpose is inferred from what the arrangement does rather than from anything the participants say," which slightly overstates - what participants say is evidence of intent, it is simply not controlling, and the related_facts entry states the point correctly as "not only from what participants say"; the two formulations should be reconciled; (c) the core_reasoning paraphrase of 247 CMR 9.01(2) renders "dispense a drug, device, or other substance" as "dispensing a drug or device," dropping "or other substance" - immaterial to the analysis; (d) 247 CMR 9.01(2) is framed in terms of intent, and while the stem supplies facts sufficient to establish the prohibited manner, neither the explanation nor the rule record notes that 247 CMR 9.01(4) (practice within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice) reaches the same conduct without any intent finding, which would make the keyed reasoning more robust; (e) reasoning_steps entry 2, "Confirm the planned service falls outside the pharmacist-administration routes in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1," is not a step a candidate can actually perform on this stem, because the stem stipulates that premise and names no medication - the declared reasoning path is wider than the item as written. ACTOR, SCOPE AND JURISDICTION PRECISION: actor attribution is precise throughout - the protocol has the pharmacist complete the sale and give the injection, the patient holds the syringe, and choice E squarely raises the individual-versus-designer question, which the authorities resolve against the individual licensee. Jurisdiction is correctly Massachusetts and the operative authority is a Massachusetts Board regulation. The scope limitation worth recording is that the stem stipulates rather than tests the Massachusetts-specific administration premise, so the item's Massachusetts content is asserted rather than exercised; that is an item-construct matter and is adjudicated in the companion realism record, where it contributes to a FAIL. ANTI-CIRCUMVENTION REASONING: sound. The item reconstructs the integrated transaction, asks what independent clinical or handling function the intermediate step performs, finds none (no preparation, storage or handling role, no interval, identical for every patient), and treats that absence as evidence of the manner the regulation prohibits. That is the correct analytical move under a standard that reaches the manner of an arrangement and expressly covers indirect circumvention, and it does not overreach into asserting that any dispensing-then-administering sequence is unlawful.
results.Proposed_Answer: C - unchanged. The keyed answer is correct and no change to the key is warranted. On the authorities verified above, C is the only defensible selection: A is defeated by 247 CMR 9.01(2)'s reach to the manner of an arrangement and by the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 definition of "Dispense" as including administering; B is defeated by the stem's own statement that the pharmacist gives the injection, read against the s. 1 "Administer" definition, whose operative act is direct application to the body; D is defeated by the closed enumeration in s. 1(c), under which a prescription supports only routes (ii) and (iii); and E is defeated by 247 CMR 10.01 and 10.03(1), which reach an individual registered pharmacist and list conduct beyond the authorized pharmacist scope as a free-standing ground.
results.Proposed_Rewrite: No legal rewrite is required and none is performed here; this field describes only what a repair would have to achieve if the companion realism findings are actioned. A repair should not touch the keyed proposition, the rule mapping, or the scenario. It would need to do three things. First, neutralise the stem's conclusory clause: "assigns the patient no preparation, storage, or handling role, sets no interval between the handover and the return, and runs the same way for every patient" states the pretext conclusion rather than supplying facts from which a candidate must infer it, and should be replaced by operational detail (for example, the protocol's stated staffing, timing and documentation instructions) from which the absence of any independent function has to be derived. Second, break the answer-polarity split: exactly one of five options says the protocol is not acceptable while the other four validate the arrangement or excuse the pharmacist, which lets a test-wise candidate select C structurally; at least one further option should become a wrong-reason "impermissible" option so that the negative polarity no longer identifies the key. Third, replace distractor B, which asserts that the patient's possession makes the patient the administering party and is refuted by the express stem fact that the pharmacist gives the injection, so it is eliminable on reading alone and contributes no discrimination. A repair that additionally named the medication and required the candidate to test it against M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1(c), 105 CMR 700.003(6) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5), instead of stipulating the restriction, would make the item test Massachusetts law rather than a general inference about sham sequencing, and would also widen its separation from MA-Q-0295. Any such rewrite would re-hash the record and would require a fresh independent audit; it is outside the scope of this review.
results.Proposed_Explanation: No replacement explanation is required; the existing explanation is accurate and its choice analysis is correct for all five options. This field records only the refinements a repair would need to make. (1) Reconcile the two statements of how purpose is established: core_reasoning's "[p]urpose is inferred from what the arrangement does rather than from anything the participants say" should be brought into line with the related_facts formulation, "not only from what participants say about it," since what the participants say is evidence of intent under 247 CMR 9.01(2) and is simply not controlling. (2) Add the independent, intent-free ground: 247 CMR 9.01(4) requires a pharmacist to practise within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice, and 247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) makes conduct beyond the authorized pharmacist scope a free-standing disciplinary ground, so the conclusion does not depend on resolving the intent question that 247 CMR 9.01(2) raises. (3) Qualify the administration-authority sentence so it cannot be read as an exhaustive map: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1(c) supplies three routes, but 105 CMR 700.001(5) and 700.003(6) authorize Department-designated immunizations and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5) permits vaccine administration under a retail collaborative practice agreement; the same qualification would improve the MA-ADMINISTER-STATUTORY-ROUTES rule record. (4) Supply the missing scheduling step - M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 3(6) places every prescription drug not otherwise scheduled in Schedule VI, which is what brings an unnamed prescription injectable inside the words "administer a controlled substance" in 247 CMR 9.01(2); the explanation currently assumes this without stating it. (5) Restore the quoted regulation to its full terms, "dispense a drug, device, or other substance," and align reasoning_steps entry 2 with the stem, which stipulates rather than requires the candidate to establish that the service falls outside the pharmacist-administration routes.
